posts.title: Poll: would you let an AI agent move 20% of your ad budget?
posts.hook: Would you let an AI agent move 20% of your ad budget without your sign-off?
posts.caption:
Would you let an AI agent move 20% of your ad budget without your sign-off?

Most people answer this on instinct, as a question about the technology. I think the answer says more about the team than the tool.

To hand over a budget decision, you have to be able to state the rule behind it. When do we cut an ad. When do we put more money behind one.

A team that has those rules written down can give them to a new hire, an agency or an agent, and check the work afterwards. A team that carries them in two people's heads cannot hand them to anyone.

So before you vote, try writing your cut rule in one sentence. If that takes more than a minute, you have found something more useful than the poll result.

posts.title: The memory test: ten questions after 12 months of ads
posts.hook: A year of ads is research you have already paid for.
posts.caption:
A year of ads is research you have already paid for.

Most teams can quote last month's RoAS. Fewer can say why their strongest ad did well, or which ads they would never run again.

Here is a test for your next review. Ten questions, laptops closed, 30 minutes. Each person writes their answers alone, then the room compares.

Seven or more answers that everyone agrees on: your brand remembers. Fewer than that: the learning is sitting in the ad account and in one or two heads.

The ten questions are in the slides. The December review is a good time to run it, while the sale is still fresh.

posts.title: Agents, not headcount: the two-column test before a hire
posts.hook: Most marketing headcount requests are requests for more hands.
posts.caption:
Most marketing headcount requests are requests for more hands.

Hands to move information from one place to another, which is the work software agents now do well.

Before I would approve another hire on a D2C marketing team, I would ask for one page: last week's hours, split into two columns.

Column one is moving information. Pulling reports, tagging creatives, rebuilding the review deck, chasing files and approvals.

Column two is deciding. What to make next, what to scale, what to stop, which risk is worth taking this quarter.

I expect the first column to be the longer one on most teams. That column is where agents belong. They do not tire on the fortieth creative.

The second column is where people belong, and it rarely gets a full day of anyone's week.

So the planning question for 2027 changes. Start with the decisions you want made better. Then ask whether each one needs a person or an agent.

Hire for the second column. Automate the first.

posts.title: A pilot without a business question is just a longer demo
posts.hook: A pilot without a business question is just a longer demo.
posts.caption:
A pilot without a business question is just a longer demo.

It runs for six weeks, everyone finds it interesting, and nobody can say what to do next.

That is an avoidable way for a software pilot to die. So here is the one-page note I would want written before any pilot starts, including a pilot with Galvor.

Line one: the question, in money terms. 'Which creative choices are raising our cost per order?' is a question. 'Let us see what the tool can do' is a tour.

Line two: the decision the answer will change, and the name of the person who will make it. If no budget or brief moves either way, do not run the pilot.

Line three: the result that would make us stop. Agree it on day one, while nobody has anything to defend.

Then put the review date in the calendar before the kick-off.

A vendor who resists that page is telling you something. A buyer who cannot fill it in is not ready yet, and it is kinder to say so early.

The page takes twenty minutes. It protects the six weeks.

posts.title: Why Galvor never touches the media budget
posts.hook: We built Galvor so it never touches your media budget.
posts.caption:
We built Galvor so it never touches your media budget.

This year many tools in our category went the other way and now launch and manage ads themselves. Here is why we have not.

The first reason is checking. When the same system recommends a move, makes the move and reports the result, nobody outside it can test the advice. We would rather give the reasoning to your team and let them argue with it.

The second is accountability. A founder answers for the marketing budget to a board and to a bank balance. That answer should not be 'the tool decided'.

So we stop at the recommendation: scale this, cut that, shift this much, and here is why. Your team or your agency moves the money.

This costs us something. A tool that acts looks faster in a demo than a tool that explains.

I accept that trade. Speed is easy to buy. An explanation your team can check is harder to find, and it is what makes the next decision better.

posts.title: Where I would never let AI make the final marketing call
posts.hook: We build AI for marketing teams. Some calls I would keep away from it.
posts.caption:
We build AI for marketing teams.
Some calls I would keep away from it.

The way I sort them is two questions.

Can we undo this within a week? And if it was wrong, would the numbers tell us?

When both answers are yes, let the agent do the reading and propose the move. Which ad is tiring. Which opening shot to test next. A mistake there shows up in the next report and gets corrected.

When either answer is no, a person makes the final call. Four examples from a D2C brand's week:

A health or results claim in an ad. Once it is seen, it cannot be withdrawn.

The price and the offer. Buyers remember a discount long after the campaign ends.

The face of the brand. Which creator or founder story stands for you is a question of trust.

Anything tied to a festival or a sensitive moment.

In each of these, the cost of being wrong does not appear on a dashboard.

A useful hour in the last week of the year: list ten decisions your team made this quarter and sort them with those two questions.
posts.notes: Hook shape: stacked. Reader: a CMO or founder deciding what to hand to AI tools in 2027. Argument: a two-question test (can we undo it in a week, would the numbers show the mistake) sorts agent calls from human calls. No statistics; 'ten decisions' and 'a week' are the exercise's own terms. Optional for Sunil: one real decision he kept with a person, added after the four examples. posts.title: AI content at scale: five checks before anything goes live
posts.hook: AI made it cheap to produce a hundred ads. Checking them is still your job.
posts.caption:
AI made it cheap to produce a hundred ads.
Checking them is still your job.

When making an ad costs almost nothing, the limit on a team moves from production to control. Without checks, a team launches many ads that look alike, and the ads compete with each other.

In Galvor's analysis of new video ads launched from May to September 2026, when six or more look-alikes launched within three days, each got 48% less first-month spend.

The slides have five checks to set up before the first batch of the year, and the one step most teams skip after the ads have run.

None of them needs new software. They need a rule and a name against it.

posts.title: The CMO of 2028 runs people, agencies and agents in one rhythm
posts.hook: By 2028 a CMO will run people, agencies and agents together.
posts.caption:
By 2028 a CMO will run people, agencies and agents together.

Today most teams run them on separate calendars, and that is where the learning gets lost.

The in-house team has a Monday review. The agency sends a monthly deck. Creators work to a campaign plan. AI tools produce whenever someone asks. Each one learns something, and none of it reaches the others in time to matter.

You do not have to wait for 2028 to fix this. Put everyone on one two-week cycle.

Before the meeting, agents do the reading: what ran, what it cost per order, what looked different about the ads that did well.

In the meeting, people decide. What to scale, what to cut, what to test next.

Within two days, those decisions go into the briefs for the agency and the creators, in the same words.

Two weeks later the cycle opens with one question: what did the last one teach us?

Two weeks is long enough for an ad to show a result and short enough that the lesson is still usable.

The CMO's job in that system is to keep the rhythm, and to make sure nothing learned in one corner stays there.

Argument: put all of them on one two-week cycle with fixed roles (agents read, people decide, briefs carry the decisions). posts.title: AI-generated vs AI-informed creative
posts.hook: Making ads got cheap. Knowing which ad to make did not.
posts.caption:
Making ads got cheap.
Knowing which ad to make did not.

Those are two different uses of AI, and brand teams tend to buy the first one.

AI-generated creative means using a tool to produce more ads, faster. AI-informed creative means using it to read what your past ads taught you, and then writing the brief.

The second is the better bet, and here is the evidence I would put in front of a founder.

In Galvor's analysis of new video ads launched from May to September 2026, a proven message shown in a new look got 47% more first-month spend. A new message over a familiar first shot got less than average.

So the most valuable brief is short: keep this message, change how it looks. You can only write it if you know which of your messages is proven.

A check for your next batch. For every ad, fill in two blanks. The message is kept from which earlier ad? What will look different?

If the first blank stays empty, you are generating blind, whichever tool you use.

Decide what to make first. After that, the tool matters much less.

posts.title: Five questions to ask any AI marketing vendor, including us
posts.hook: Five questions to ask any AI marketing vendor. Ask us too.
posts.caption:
Five questions to ask any AI marketing vendor. Ask us too.

A demo shows a product on its best day. These questions show the other days.

They cover what the vendor refuses to do, whether the product can explain itself, where it goes wrong, what you keep if you leave, and whose working week has to change.

Send them before the demo and ask for the answers in writing. A written answer gets checked by more people than a spoken one, and you can hold it against the contract later.

The five are in the slides. I would want Galvor held to the same list.

slides.headline: *Five questions* to ask any AI marketing vendor. Including us.
slides.sub: Send them first. Ask for the answers in writing.

slides.headline: What do you *refuse* to do?
slides.body:
Clear limits tell you what a product is for.

A good answer names something the vendor has chosen not to build. 'We do everything' is a warning.

slides.headline: Can it show *why*, in words my team can check?
slides.body:
Ask to see the reasoning behind one recommendation.

If your growth lead cannot argue with it, they cannot trust it either.

slides.headline: What does it *get wrong*, and how would we know?
slides.body:
Every system has blind spots.

A vendor who knows theirs can tell you where a person still has to check the work.

slides.headline: What do we *keep* if we leave?
slides.body:
Your ads taught the system something.

Ask what you can take with you: the tags, the findings, the history. Get it in writing.

slides.headline: Whose *week* changes, and how?
slides.body:
A tool that changes nobody's routine changes nothing.

Ask which meeting, which report and which person will work differently in the first month.

slides.headline: Send these *before* your next demo
slides.sub: Save the list. Ask for written answers.

posts.title: AI can make average marketing look busy
posts.hook: AI can make an average marketing team look very productive.
posts.caption:
AI can make an average marketing team look very productive.

The output goes up. What the team knows about its buyers stays where it was.

This is the risk I would watch in 2027, more than any risk to jobs. If your weekly report counts creatives shipped, posts published and decks sent, AI will improve every line on it. The report will look better while the business stays the same.

The fix is one change to that report.

Remove the line that counts what was made. Add a line that counts questions answered.

A question is answered when a test ends in a decision: scale it, cut it, or change the brief. A test that ends in 'interesting' counts as zero.

Then read the number every fortnight. A team that ships forty ads and answers one question has had a slow fortnight. A team that ships eight and answers four has had a good one.

Output is what you paid for. A decision is what you got for the money.

Count the second one, and AI becomes useful for the right reason.

posts.title: Before approving next year's budget: the one-page learning note
posts.hook: Before you approve next year's marketing budget, ask for one page.
posts.caption:
Before you approve next year's marketing budget, ask for one page.

It answers one question: what did this year's ads teach us, in rupees?

February is when most plans for the new financial year get drafted. The usual draft is last year's number plus a percentage, split by channel. It says where the money will go. It does not say what the last twelve months of spend found out.

So ask the marketing team for three lines.

What will we stop paying for, and which ads showed us that?

What will we pay more for, and which ads showed us that?

What do we still not know, and how much are we setting aside to find out?

The third line matters most to a finance head. It turns 'testing' from a habit into a named amount with a question attached, and a named amount can be reviewed.

If the team cannot fill in the first two lines, last year's budget bought sales and no knowledge. Next year's plan is then the same bet at a higher price.

A budget that starts from what was learned is easier to defend, and easier to cut well.

posts.title: Human judgement is the product. So who is training it?
posts.hook: Agents are taking the work junior marketers used to learn on.
posts.caption:
Agents are taking the work junior marketers used to learn on.

So judgement, which used to build up by itself, now has to be taught on purpose.

Pulling reports and tagging ads by hand was dull work. It was also how a new marketer saw hundreds of ads next to their numbers and slowly learned what good looks like. When an agent does that work, the senior people keep their judgement and the next group never forms theirs.

Two habits a team can start this week.

Call first, then look. Before anyone opens the agent's recommendation, each person writes their own call on the ad in one line: scale, cut or test, and why. Then compare. The gaps are the lesson.

Review one miss a fortnight. Take a decision that went wrong and trace what was known on the day it was made. The aim is to find the reasoning that failed, never to find a person to blame.

Both take under an hour, and neither needs a new tool.

Human judgement is the product. Agents are the leverage. Leverage on untrained judgement only gets a team to the wrong answer sooner.
